doc.title: Jane Monheit interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, August 20, 2010

title: Contracts, lawyer and record sales
summary: Basic contract with options, a lawyer handling it, and why jazz musicians make money on the road rather than from recoupment.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Well for that record, you signed a contract with this company, was it for a certain number of recordings, was it a one-shot deal sort of?

Yeah as I recall it was pretty much your basic contract, you know, you do an album and then you have like options after that, like five options or so. You know I’ve never been too — I’ve got a very good lawyer. He handles it. I know a little bit about that side of things, as much as I really need to know, but mostly I focus on music and you know, just being really involved with the planning and imaging and touring and all of that sort of stuff that happens. I’m involved with all of it now but I wasn’t back then.
Okay. That was sort of my next question, you have to have a lawyer to sort of look at contracts.
And don’t fall into that classic trap of — there was decades of musicians being taken advantage of.
Oh yeah, yeah — no. I’ve never been taken advantage of, luckily. Never.
Do record sales have an impact on how much money you make?

As a jazz musician on my level no, not at all. We make our money on the road. If you are a big star with just amazing success, you know, a Harry Connick Jr. or a Diana Krall, and your records are going platinum and you have this amazing fan base that just supports you no matter what, then you’re going to make some money off your records, yeah. And if you’ve got publishing too.
Is that because they are in the position where they can have it in their contact with the record company that they will get a percentage of sales or something like that?
Well yeah, after the record recoups.

Yeah. That’ll be part of you contract, part of anyone’s contract. But it’s hard to recoup on an expensive jazz record, when people aren’t really buying CDs that often. I mean we sell them more on the road now because people aren’t buying them in the stores anymore, they’re downloading them from iTunes, and they’ll buy one on the road because they want you to sign it. You know I’ll sit there and talk with everybody and sign the records and hang out. I love talking to the crowd after the shows. I mean it’s nice. I get to thank everybody. It’s a nice thing. But yeah, we’ll sell records at the show for that reason. So
it’s hard to recoup, we’re not selling — you know nobody’s selling a ton of records right now. The pop stars are selling less than they ever did.
